title: GB-0669, an AI-designed anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibody, completed a randomized first-in-human trial
summary: In a phase 1 trial in 51 healthy adults, GB-0669, an antibody optimized with Generate Biomedicines' machine-learning models, was tolerated, had a 54-day half-life and neutralized virus in serum.
account: Generate Biomedicines used machine-learning models and laboratory testing to optimize the antibody that became GB-0669. The original design study describes a structure-conditioned generative model followed by sequence-to-function models trained on experimental results. The phase 1 trial began on 18 July 2023, according to the sponsor's registry entry. It enrolled 51 healthy adults in Orlando, with 36 receiving GB-0669 and 15 receiving placebo across five dose groups. Company staff presented interim results at IDWeek on 17 October 2024. Their abstract states that each dose cohort was randomized to GB-0669 or placebo. The trial was completed on 22 November 2024, according to the registry entry. The registry entry was first posted after the study ended. Its structured allocation field says that the trial was nonrandomized, and the manuscript describes randomization. That inconsistency remains unresolved. The results appeared as an author preprint on 8 October 2025 and in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in July 2026. The authors reported no dose-limiting toxicity and no serious adverse events. One grade 2 infusion reaction led to interruption of the infusion. Serum testing showed dose-dependent live-virus neutralization at 600 and 1,200 mg. These were laboratory tests of participant serum. They do not show that patients avoided infection or recovered from illness. The authors propose a phase 2 trial at 1,200 mg in immunocompromised people. As of 29 October 2026, no later GB-0669 trial is registered.
purpose: Use generative machine learning to design a therapeutic antibody against a conserved, poorly immunogenic region of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein.

display.answer: Generate Biomedicines staff wrote or co-wrote every cited source. Company staff presented interim results at IDWeek on 17 October 2024. The full clinical results appeared as the authors' preprint of 8 October 2025 and then in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in July 2026. The machine-learning design traces to a separate company preprint of 31 March 2025. The structured allocation field of the registry entry says that the trial was nonrandomized, and the IDWeek abstract and the paper describe randomization.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: In a phase 1 trial in 51 healthy adults, GB-0669, an antibody optimized with Generate Biomedicines' machine-learning models, was tolerated, had a 54-day half-life and neutralized virus in serum.
fields.account: Generate Biomedicines used machine-learning models and laboratory testing to optimize the antibody that became GB-0669. The original design study describes a structure-conditioned generative model followed by sequence-to-function models trained on experimental results. The phase 1 trial began on 18 July 2023, according to the sponsor's registry entry. It enrolled 51 healthy adults in Orlando, with 36 receiving GB-0669 and 15 receiving placebo across five dose groups. Company staff presented interim results at IDWeek on 17 October 2024. Their abstract states that each dose cohort was randomized to GB-0669 or placebo. The trial was completed on 22 November 2024, according to the registry entry. The registry entry was first posted after the study ended. Its structured allocation field says that the trial was nonrandomized, and the manuscript describes randomization. That inconsistency remains unresolved. The results appeared as an author preprint on 8 October 2025 and in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in July 2026. The authors reported no dose-limiting toxicity and no serious adverse events. One grade 2 infusion reaction led to interruption of the infusion. Serum testing showed dose-dependent live-virus neutralization at 600 and 1,200 mg. These were laboratory tests of participant serum. They do not show that patients avoided infection or recovered from illness. The authors propose a phase 2 trial at 1,200 mg in immunocompromised people. As of 29 October 2026, no later GB-0669 trial is registered.
